Constraint enforcement operates largely independently of the extraction model's intrinsic capability: it restricts the output space to ontologically valid triples regardless of the underlying model's accuracy.
When applied to fine-tuned models that reach competitive F1 levels, the same constraints remain necessary---Phase~0 analysis confirms that even well-prompted models exhibit non-trivial violation rates (15.37\% DR on SciERC, 18.46\% on DocRED).
% exp_ids: phase0_scierc_unconstrained, phase2_docred_unconstrained
In our evaluation, F1 serves as a \emph{control variable} verifying that constraint enforcement does not degrade extraction quality, not as an optimization target.
The contribution of this work is the constraint enforcement method itself; the zero-shot setting isolates its effect from confounds introduced by task-specific fine-tuning.

%          phase2_docred_full_s1 (CF=2.57%)

\paragraph{Severity of Cross-Field Violations.}
Domain/range (DR) violations produce structurally invalid triples---a triple asserting that a \emph{Task} entity fills the \emph{domain} slot of \textsc{Part-of}, which requires \emph{Method}, cannot be consumed by any downstream system without error.
DR violations are therefore hard constraints.
Cross-field consistency (CF) violations are qualitatively different: each individual triple remains type-valid with respect to its own relation's domain/range rules; only cross-triple consistency is broken when the same entity receives different types across relations.
The dominant conflict pattern---\emph{Generic}$\leftrightarrow$\emph{OtherScientificTerm} (60 of 245~affected entities on SciERC)---reflects genuine semantic ambiguity in the type system rather than a systematic method failure.
% exp_id: phase2_scierc_full_s1
Ablation evidence cleanly attributes CF to the semantic layer: grammar-only decoding yields CF\,=\,0.08\%, matching the unconstrained baseline, while the full system reaches 9.90\% on SciERC and 2.57\% on DocRED
(Qwen3-8B; Llama-3.1-8B exhibits 12.02\% on DocRED, the highest across all configurations).

\begin{abstract}
LLM-based information extraction systems produce systematic ontology constraint violations during autoregressive generation.
On SciERC (7 relation types), 15.37\% of extracted triples violate domain/range type constraints; on DocRED (96 relation types), 18.46\%.
Violation rates are governed by \emph{constraint tightness} ($\bar{\tau}$, the fraction of type-pair space ruled out per relation): DocRED ($\bar{\tau}{=}0.842$, mean 5.68 valid pairs) and SciERC ($\bar{\tau}{=}0.333$, mean 24 valid pairs) exhibit comparable violation rates despite a 14$\times$ difference in ontology size.
%
We present \textsc{OntoCoDec}, which compiles IE ontology schemas into two composable decoding constraint layers:
(1)~a \emph{grammar layer} (XGrammar CFG) enforcing JSON structural validity and restricting entity-type and relation vocabularies to schema-defined values (ET, RV\,$\to$\,0\%); and
(2)~a \emph{semantic layer} (TypeConstraintProcessor) enforcing domain/range constraints via a stateful entity registry and dynamic logit masking.
The grammar layer is an enabling prerequisite; the two compose via bitwise AND on token-level masks.
%
On SciERC, \textsc{OntoCoDec} reduces domain/range violations by 94\% (15.37\%\,$\to$\,0.93\%) while maintaining extraction F1 ({+}0.13pp, $p{=}0.58$, not significant).
On DocRED, violations decrease by 45\% (18.46\%\,$\to$\,10.21\%) with significant gains in relation F1 ({+}0.50pp, $p{<}0.001$) and entity F1 ({+}1.23pp, $p{<}0.001$) for Qwen3-8B; Llama-3.1-8B shows comparable violation reduction with F1-neutral impact. % exp_ids: phase2_docred_full, llama_docred_full_s1, llama_docred_unconstrained
Results are validated across two models (Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct) and two datasets.
Compared with post-hoc filtering, decoding-time enforcement preserves true positives and eliminates entity-type violations that post-hoc methods cannot address.
\end{abstract}

13	SciERC ($\bar{\tau}{=}0.333$, mean 24 valid type pairs per relation) and DocRED ($\bar{\tau}{=}0.842$, mean 5.68) exhibit comparable violation rates despite a 14$\times$ difference in ontology size, and within each model, DR reduction scales inversely with $\bar{\tau}$: 94--99\% on SciERC ($\bar{\tau}{=}0.333$) vs.\ 45--90\% on DocRED ($\bar{\tau}{=}0.842$), with the residual modulated by model-specific baseline violation rates (Section~\ref{sec:cross-model}).
14	% Qwen: SciERC DR↓94%, DocRED DR↓45%; Llama: SciERC DR↓99%, DocRED DR↓90%
15	
16	Second, we introduced a two-layer constraint architecture that decomposes ontological enforcement into complementary mechanisms:
17	a \emph{grammar layer} (XGrammar CFG) that eliminates structural violations (RV, ET\,$\to$\,0\%) and a \emph{semantic layer} (TypeConstraintProcessor with a stateful entity registry) that enforces domain/range constraints at the token level. % exp_id: phase2_scierc_grammar_only
18	The grammar layer serves as an enabling prerequisite for the semantic layer; the two compose via bitwise AND over candidate token sets.
19	
20	Third, we validated OntoCoDec empirically.
21	On SciERC, the full system reduces domain/range violations from 15.37\% to 0.93\%---a 94\% relative reduction---while completely eliminating RV and ET violations, with no significant impact on relation F1 ($+$0.13 percentage points, $p > 0.05$). % exp_id: phase2_scierc_full_s1

23	Compared with post-hoc filtering, decoding-time enforcement preserves true positives and eliminates entity-type violations that post-hoc methods cannot address.
24	
25	\paragraph{Limitations.}
26	Several limitations qualify these findings.
27	The semantic layer introduces cross-field consistency (CF) violations: CF rises from 0.08\% under unconstrained decoding to 9.90\% with full constraints. % exp_ids: phase2_scierc_unconstrained, phase2_scierc_full_s1
28	This is a systematic consequence of per-relation independent type enforcement---when the same entity appears across multiple triples, each relation's domain/range constraint may assign it a different type, producing entity-versus-relation type drift.
29	The grammar layer alone does not elevate CF (0.08\%, matching the unconstrained baseline), confirming that CF is entirely attributable to the semantic layer. % exp_id: phase2_scierc_grammar_only
30	Resolving this cross-relation type coherence problem is an open challenge, not a trivial implementation fix.
31	Cross-field consistency violations increase with constraint strength and vary across models: CF reaches 12.02\% for Llama-3.1-8B on DocRED under full constraints, compared with 2.57\% for Qwen3-8B on the same dataset, suggesting that per-relation independent enforcement interacts with model-specific generation patterns. % exp_ids: llama_docred_full_s1, phase2_docred_full

All F1 metrics are computed over successfully parsed documents only. % exp_ids: llama_docred_full_s1, llama_docred_unconstrained

34	% llama_docred_unconstrained: DR=26.07%; llama_docred_full_s1: DR=2.55%
35	Results are reported for two models and two datasets under zero-shot prompting only, and integration with fine-tuned models has not been explored.
36	
37	\paragraph{Future Work.}
38	We identify four directions.
39	(1)~Extension to larger models (quantized 70B-class) to further verify model-agnostic generalization across scales.
40	(2)~Global entity-level type consensus during decoding---maintaining a shared entity registry across all relations within an instance---to resolve CF violations.
41	(3)~Integration with fine-tuned models, combining constraint-aware training objectives with decoding-time enforcement.
42	(4)~Extension to non-English ontologies to evaluate cross-lingual applicability.

Our work makes three contributions.

First, we conducted the first systematic study of ontological constraint violations in LLM-based IE (\S\ref{sec:violation_landscape}).
Across two benchmarks with substantially different ontology sizes---SciERC (7~relations) and DocRED (96~relations)---we found that domain/range violation rates are comparable (15.37\% vs.\ 18.46\%), % exp_ids: phase0_scierc_unconstrained, phase0_docred_unconstrained

% Qwen: SciERC DR↓94%, DocRED DR↓45%; Llama: SciERC DR↓99%, DocRED DR↓90%

Second, we introduced a two-layer constraint architecture that decomposes ontological enforcement into complementary mechanisms:
a \emph{grammar layer} (XGrammar CFG) that eliminates structural violations (RV, ET\,$\to$\,0\%) and a \emph{semantic layer} (TypeConstraintProcessor with a stateful entity registry) that enforces domain/range constraints at the token level. % exp_id: phase2_scierc_grammar_only
The grammar layer serves as an enabling prerequisite for the semantic layer; the two compose via bitwise AND over candidate token sets.

Third, we validated OntoCoDec empirically.
On SciERC, the full system reduces domain/range violations from 15.37\% to 0.93\%---a 94\% relative reduction---while completely eliminating RV and ET violations, with no significant impact on relation F1 ($+$0.13 percentage points, $p > 0.05$). % exp_id: phase2_scierc_full_s1

Llama-3.1-8B achieves comparable DR reduction (90.2\%, 26.07\%\,$\to$\,2.55\%) with F1-neutral impact. % exp_ids: phase2_docred_full, llama_docred_full_s1, llama_docred_unconstrained
Compared with post-hoc filtering, decoding-time enforcement preserves true positives and eliminates entity-type violations that post-hoc methods cannot address.

\paragraph{Limitations.}
Several limitations qualify these findings.
The semantic layer introduces cross-field consistency (CF) violations: CF rises from 0.08\% under unconstrained decoding to 9.90\% with full constraints. % exp_ids: phase2_scierc_unconstrained, phase2_scierc_full_s1
This is a systematic consequence of per-relation independent type enforcement---when the same entity appears across multiple triples, each relation's domain/range constraint may assign it a different type, producing entity-versus-relation type drift.
The grammar layer alone does not elevate CF (0.08\%, matching the unconstrained baseline), confirming that CF is entirely attributable to the semantic layer. % exp_id: phase2_scierc_grammar_only

% llama_docred_unconstrained: DR=26.07%; llama_docred_full_s1: DR=2.55%
Results are reported for two models and two datasets under zero-shot prompting only, and integration with fine-tuned models has not been explored.

\paragraph{Future Work.}
We identify four directions.
(1)~Extension to larger models (quantized 70B-class) to further verify model-agnostic generalization across scales.
(2)~Global entity-level type consensus during decoding---maintaining a shared entity registry across all relations within an instance---to resolve CF violations.
(3)~Integration with fine-tuned models, combining constraint-aware training objectives with decoding-time enforcement.
